t: Minimum Operations to Transform Binary String — Left-to-Right DP
o: We must turn s1 into s2 using two moves: flip a single '0' to '1' (cost 1), or destroy an adjacent "11" into "00" (cost 1). Crucially, a '1' can only be removed by pairing it with a neighboring '1', and that neighbor may need to be created (paid for) or repaired afterward (paid for) if its own target is '1'. In Example 2 ("01" -> "10") we pay 1 to build the partner, 1 for the pair, and 1 to restore index 0, totaling 3. In Example 3 a lone '1' with target '0' has no way to disappear, hence -1. With n up to 1e5 we need a linear scan rather than search.
k: A '1' that must become '0' can only die inside a pair operation, so it needs a neighbor that is '1' at that moment.
Creating or repairing a partner each costs exactly one extra operation, which suggests carrying a small state along a scan.
Each index participates in at most one pair operation in an optimal plan, enabling a left-to-right DP.

a.i: Treat every reachable string as a graph node and BFS from s1 until s2 appears. This directly models the operations and is easy to reason about, but the state space is exponential, so it only serves as intuition and works for tiny inputs.
s: Put s1 in a queue with distance 0.
Pop a string; if it equals s2 return its distance.
Generate all strings obtainable by one operation and push unseen ones.
a.t: Exponential in n — states are all reachable binary strings; only viable for tiny n.

a.i: Scan left to right. Let dp[v] be the minimum cost after settling positions 0..i-1 such that they already match s2 and position i currently holds bit v. From each state we either finish index i without a pair (free if v equals s2[i], or cost 1 if v=0 and s2[i]=1), or perform a pair (i, i+1): pay to raise i to '1' if needed, pay to raise the partner if s1[i+1]='0', pay 1 for the pair itself, and pay 1 more to restore i if s2[i]='1'. The pair leaves position i+1 as '0', giving the next state. This captures every optimal plan because an optimal solution never needs an index in two pair operations.
s: For each i from 0 to n-2, build the next dp: no-pair transition (cost 0 or 1) into state s1[i+1], and pair transition (build costs + pair + optional restore) into state 0.
The answer is dp[s2[n-1]] after the scan, or -1 if infinite.
All transitions are O(1), so the scan is linear.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with constant work per position.
a.sp: O(1) — only two DP values are kept at a time.

w: Use the DP in an interview; mention BFS only to show you understand the operation semantics. Pitfalls: forgetting the +1 for the pair operation itself, forgetting to restore a paired index whose target is '1', and mishandling n = 1 (answer 0 if equal, else -1). Follow-ups: prove an index never joins two pair operations optimally, or reconstruct the actual operation sequence by storing parent choices.
